transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-07
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 1:18
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Anya Kothari (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (AcroLabs), Luke Chen (AcroLabs), Marta Gomez (AcroLabs CTO), Benji Ortiz (AcroLabs SRE)

Summary:
We walked through AcroLabs' on-prem inference workload profile, discussed kernel-selection nondeterminism observed when toggling quantization and CUDA graph replay, and proposed a 3-stage kernel-snapshot + trace run on their 8xA100 cluster. Customer is leaning toward an on-prem Dedicated pilot but has security and latency SLO concerns; they want concrete traces and a short pilot scope.

Topics covered:
- Kernel heuristics snapshotting and what we look for (launch configs, warp occupancy, shared mem footprints)
- Differences observed between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths under mixed batching and KV cache pressure
- CUDA graph replay instability when KV cache is persistent across requests vs cold starts
- Quantization toggles (int8 dynamic vs q4_0 style) and their effect on kernel selection
- VPC/on-prem networking jitter impact on scheduling and batching windows
- Pilot scope, security artifacts, and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for the time today, happy friday, we'll try to be crisp. Diego and Anya from the SE side are with me to dig into the kernel-level stuff you flagged in your ticket.
[00:12] Priya (AcroLabs): Thanks Samira, appreciate it. We've been seeing some weird latency spikes when we turn on quantization and also when we warm the KV cache, like tail latency jumps to the 95th then 99th.
[00:25] Diego (Redwood SE): Got it. Can you give us a quick stack summary? Are you on our Dedicated product or running a private on-prem runtime?
[00:33] Luke (AcroLabs): We're on-prem, using our own Kubernetes cluster with direct NVLink between the eight A100s. We're testing both your TRT-LLM plugin and vLLM open runtime. Base images are linux 5.15, drivers 535.xx.
[00:46] Anya (Redwood SE): Do you have persistent KV cache enabled across requests? That changes the execution path a lot.
[00:52] Benji (AcroLabs SRE): Yeah we persisted the cache to get better prefix reuse. But at scale the eviction behavior + cuda-graph replay seems to sometimes pick a fallback kernel path.
[01:05] Diego (Redwood SE): That's consistent with what we've seen: when the KV cache footprint grows and CUDA graphs are replayed with different shapes, the runtime sometimes switches to a different kernel path mid-flight, which can increase latency because of kernel compilation or launch config mismatches.
[01:19] Priya (AcroLabs): Does that happen more on TRT-LLM or vLLM? We saw different behavior across both.
[01:25] Diego (Redwood SE): Good question. TRT-LLM tends to prefer fused kernels and will fall back to less optimal kernels if the workspace or shared memory requirements don't match at replay time. vLLM's dynamic execution hits a different code path — it's more resilient in some cases but can have more kernel diversity which complicates the profiling.
[01:40] Marta (CTO): And quantization? We toggled to int8 and saw better throughput but more tail latency variance.
[01:47] Anya (Redwood SE): Quantization changes both the compute kernels and memory layout. For int8 fast paths you get specialized GEMM and attention kernels that assume specific packing; when the runtime detects misaligned shapes or an unexpected sequence length, it sometimes routes to a fallback kernel that is slower. That can explain the spikes.
[02:03] Samira (Redwood AE): Quick qualification: what's your target SLO and your expected qps on the pilot?
[02:09] Priya (AcroLabs): 200 qps average, p99 under 400ms. For some interactive features we need p50 ~ 60ms.
[02:17] Samira (Redwood AE): Thanks. Ok Diego can you walk us through the snapshot approach we discussed?
[02:22] Diego (Redwood SE): Sure. We propose a three-stage snapshot: 1) cold start microtrace capturing kernel launches, occupancies, and shared memory usage across representative prompts; 2) warm KV cache snapshot with CUDA graph capture on replay to see whether replayed graphs are identical and whether launch configs change; 3) stress run under realistic arrival processes to surface interference and batching windows.
[02:41] Priya (AcroLabs): For stage 2, when you say "capture CUDA graph" do you mean exact replay or just a perf snapshot? We've had graphs be non-replayable in production because of dynamic shapes.
[02:52] Diego (Redwood SE): We mean capturing the graph replay attempt and the kernel sequence that the runtime chooses. We'll instrument to record the graph signature hash, kernel names, and the nvtx ranges. There will be some graphs that can't be replayed 1:1 but the signatures tell us when the runtime diverged.
[03:06] Benji (AcroLabs SRE): Are you going to use Nsight or your internal tracer? We prefer raw Nsight traces to correlate with our infra metrics.
[03:12] Anya (Redwood SE): We'll run both: a lightweight runtime-level snapshot from Redwood's side and a full Nsight capture you can keep for deeper perf analysis. We'll coordinate so Nsight captures the same time window.
[03:22] Priya (AcroLabs): One more question: could VPC or network jitter cause kernel-choice problems? We have a hybrid scheduler that sometimes delays batches slightly.
[03:30] Diego (Redwood SE): Indirectly yes. Scheduling jitter changes the batching window which alters sequence length distributions in a batch and can flip the runtime's heuristic that picks kernel variants. So network-induced microbursts can cascade into kernel-switching behavior.
[03:44] Marta (CTO): Hmm. That suggests a mitigations list we can consider: deterministic batching windows, tighter autoscale thresholds, or pinning model variants.
[03:53] Samira (Redwood AE): Right — Redwood can also suggest a quantization profile that keeps more shapes stable to avoid fallback paths.
[03:59] Priya (AcroLabs): About the quantization profiles — are you recommending dynamic int8 or a mixed q4/q8 approach?
[04:06] Anya (Redwood SE): For your model family we usually start with a mixed approach: keep critical attention kernels in higher precision, quantize feed-forward blocks. That reduces kernel diversity while keeping quality. We'll give you two suggested profiles to test.
[04:18] Luke (Infra): For the kernel snapshots, what's the overhead? We have production traffic, we can't take down the service.
[04:25] Diego (Redwood SE): The lightweight snapshots are low overhead — we're sampling at fine granularity but not instrumenting every call. The full Nsight trace is heavier and we recommend running that in a staging window or throttled traffic window.
[04:38] Priya (AcroLabs): Ok. Can you also explain the thing you mentioned earlier about "kernel compilation" — are we hitting JIT compiles at runtime? We thought all kernels were prebuilt.
[04:48] Diego (Redwood SE): Most kernels are precompiled, but some fused or specialized kernels get selected with specific launch parameters. When shapes change in a way the runtime hasn't seen, the path may trigger a different kernel variant which can require more expensive setup or use suboptimal launch configs. It's less "JIT compile" and more "variant selection and different occupancy."
[05:05] Samira (Redwood AE): Let's talk success criteria: what would convince you to run a Dedicated pilot?
[05:10] Marta (CTO): If we see stable p99 under 400ms with quantization enabled and no unexplained kernel-switch jumps in the warm runs, plus security controls we need (SSO, audit logs, KMS), then yes.
[05:23] Samira (Redwood AE): Noted. Diego, can you give a quick timeline for the snapshot deliverables?
[05:28] Diego (Redwood SE): We can run the initial lightweight snapshot within 48 hours of getting the prompt set and a short sampler. Nsight capture will need a scheduled window; ideally next week. We'll analyze and return findings in 5 business days after capture.
[05:42] Priya (AcroLabs): One more subtle symptom — we've seen higher memory fragmentation with mixed-precision which sometimes leads to kernel eviction and host fallback. Any thoughts?
[05:52] Anya (Redwood SE): Memory fragmentation is real, especially on long-lived processes. The runtime has heuristics for pooling, but quantized kernels have different scratchpad sizes. We'll look for patterns in the snapshot: contiguous allocations, fragmentation counters, and tracer marks.
[06:06] Benji (AcroLabs SRE): Is there anything in Redwood's Dedicated product that gives us more deterministic behavior than a vanilla on-prem deployment?
[06:14] Diego (Redwood SE): Dedicated pools are tuned (kernel selection heuristics, kernel pre-warming, and pinned model variants). Also Redwood's routing layer can avoid region or host-level bursts that trigger eviction. On-prem you can get similar behavior but it needs some tuned configs and the runtime agent.
[06:29] Samira (Redwood AE): Pricing question was in the thread: do we want to scope a small reserved capacity for pilot?
[06:36] Marta (CTO): We'll consider a short pilot agreement if the numbers add up. Please include pilot pricing in the follow-up.
[06:42] Samira (Redwood AE): Will do.
[06:47] Priya (AcroLabs): Could you talk through a concrete example: a 4-request batch with one long prefix — how would TRT-LLM vs vLLM behave?
[06:56] Diego (Redwood SE): Sure. TRT-LLM will try to choose a fused attention kernel optimized for the most common sequence length in the batch; if one request has a long prefix it may opt for a kernel that supports variable seq but with larger shared mem. vLLM might split the batch or schedule different kernels per request more aggressively which avoids large shared mem but increases kernel-switches and per-token latency.
[07:16] Priya (AcroLabs): So it's a tradeoff: one fused kernel with higher throughput but risk of heavy tail vs per-request kernels that are steadier but less throughput.
[07:22] Anya (Redwood SE): Exactly. That's why the snapshots look at both per-kernel latency histograms and the distribution of kernel variants chosen.
[07:33] Marta (CTO): Any chance we can get a small shim to force a specific kernel path for testing?
[07:39] Diego (Redwood SE): We can provide a debug flag in a staging runtime to bias the heuristic; not recommended in prod but useful for triage.
[07:46] Priya (AcroLabs): Ok that's useful.
[07:50] Samira (Redwood AE): Let's move to risks: any security or compliance concerns with Nsight traces?
[07:56] Anya (Redwood SE): Nsight traces can include pointers and low-level addresses — we recommend running it in a controlled window and shredding traces after analysis. Redwood will sign an NDA if needed.
[08:08] Luke (Infra): We use strict access controls; we'll only provide a secure host for the trace.
[08:12] Diego (Redwood SE): Great. We'll also provide a sanitized trace option that strips PII and hostnames.
[08:18] Priya (AcroLabs): On the topic of fallback paths: is there a way to quantify the cost of a kernel switch event? Like a metric we can alert on?
[08:26] Diego (Redwood SE): Yes, we instrument kernel path divergence and can emit metrics: kernel_variant_switch_count, median_switch_penalty_ms, and p99_latency_with_switches. We'll propose thresholds for alerts.
[08:38] Samira (Redwood AE): Okay let's recap actions — we'll pull the recording into the shared deal room and Samira will share security and pricing. Diego and Anya will run the snapshots once Priya shares the prompt set.
[08:51] Priya (AcroLabs): Sounds good. We'll aim to get you the prompt set and a sampler script by Monday.
[08:56] Marta (CTO): Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[09:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Thanks all, we'll follow up with meeting notes and the next call scheduling.

(Transcription notes: occasional words garbled, e.g., TRT-LLM sometimes transcribed as "TRT LLM" or "T R T L M"; kernel names are high-level and not full symbol names; some timestamps approximate.)
